title: Cannabis and Democracy. It’s Complicated.

content_html_sanitized:
If there is anything that almost everyone everywhere agrees on, it is that democracy is in crisis, but almost no one would think that cannabis is a central issue.

 

Let me explain why they are wrong.

 

Very, simply, Democracy is - by definition - about “process”. The subject may be about taxes, or the next president, or war and peace, Or it may even be about whether we allow people to use a plant to save their lives. Silly me! You can’t be serious!

 

But how do we decide whatever it is that we want to decide? Before we even get to the democratic process? What is an appropriate process?

 

When I complain that “the best two word explanation for cannabis prohibition is “bad journalism”, I am talking about more than sloppy reporting.

 

The problem goes far beyond that. What is going on with the democratic process?

 

Recently, I reported on the absurdity of France’s thirty year process of almost getting a medical cannabis program.

See

France Making An Even Bigger Mess of Its Cannabis Policy, But Finally About to Legalize Medical After Only Thirty Years

 

France certainly considers itself a functioning democracy.

 

And then there is the grotesque process in the UK that kept children with a severe form of epilepsy from getting medical cannabis.

See

Why Is the UK Still Failing Children Who Need Medical Cannabis?

 

In other words, even when everyone is in favor of even the most basic program, it is still extremely difficult to get anything done. Why?

 

If someone thinks that it is important to keep cannabis in the black market, then why aren’t we having a robust debate on it? Shouldn’t that be “newsworthy”?

 

Finally, even with all of the problems with bad journalism, and bad medical science, and bad governance it seems that a majority of the electorate in Western Europe are in favor of legalizing either medical and/or recreational cannabis.

 

In one of the great ironies of modern European politics, Germany is actually leading the way for greater personal freedom. Or maybe it is entirely appropriate. Germans learned up close about the dangers of an authoritarian state.

See Public Opinion Survey Reveals Support for Cannabis Legalization Remains Strong in Germany

 

A recent survey conducted by YouGov indicates that the legalization of cannabis in Germany continues to garner substantial public support, one year after its implementation.

And With Germany legalising cannabis, Europe is reaching a tipping point. Britain, take note

And

THE FUTURE OF CANNABIS LEGALIZATION IN EUROPE

 

In any case, leaving cannabis in the black market as the default option simply because the police and the politicians don’t want to talk about it, is irresponsible and not healthy for a democracy. (And bad journalism.)
